extracted.subtask_description: Practical, experience-based advice on novel-writing, playwriting, dealing with publishers and critics, and the discipline needed to be a working author, drawn from Trollope's memoir of his early career.

rubrics_metrics.name: No dealings with critics on one's own behalf
rubrics_metrics.description: “I would have no dealings with any critic on my own behalf. I would neither ask for nor deplore criticism, nor would I ever thank a critic for praise, or quarrel with him, even in my own heart, for censure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend this rule to young authors. Avoid touting among critics — mild suggestion to a friend can lead to crawling at the critic's feet, sending presents, and mutual understandings that are ignominious and unjust to the public. Praise obtained ignominiously is of no real value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not solicit friends to read or consult on plot; avoid reading your work aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: “I have never asked a friend to read a line; nor have I ever read a word of my own writing aloud,--even to her. With one exception ... I have never consulted a friend as to a plot, or spoken to any one of the work I have been doing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope states he kept his manuscripts private and rarely sought external plot advice; his wife was the sole regular reader. This is presented as a deliberate practice to preserve independence of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry and self-discipline are essential (early hours)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The vigour necessary to prosecute two professions at the same time is not given to every one ... There must be early hours, and I had not as yet learned to love early hours.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful sustained writing requires disciplined habits (e.g., early hours) and energy; doubting one’s industry rather than one's intellect is common. Changing habits (to find the necessary vigour) is part of the craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write what you know / rely on personal observation
rubrics_metrics.description: On failing with a historical novel: “The story is certainly inferior ... chiefly because I knew accurately the life of the people in Ireland, and knew, in truth, nothing of life in the La Vendée country.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intimate knowledge and direct observation of subjects and settings; books grounded in what the author knows are likelier to succeed artistically (and perhaps commercially).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect commercial failure; manage expectations with publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Trollope repeatedly expected nothing from early books: “Many a young author expects much from such an undertaking. I can with truth declare that I expected nothing. And I got nothing.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not count on immediate financial reward. Publisher arrangements (e.g., half-profits) often yield little. Authors should be prepared for poor sales and should not be disheartened from continuing to write.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors should take responsibility for publicity and popularization
rubrics_metrics.description: “Any efforts which might be made for the popularity of a book ought to have come from the author;--but I took in good part Mr. Colburn's assurance that he could not encourage me in the career I had commenced.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope implies that publicity and efforts to find readers are primarily the author's business; one should not rely solely on the publisher or on friends to secure readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware publisher delay and payment terms; prefer present payment if possible
rubrics_metrics.description: On publishers and payments: examples of delayed or non-existent accounts and small future payments; “If you will only make the payment future instead of present, you may generally twist a few pounds in your own or your client's favour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious in contracts; publishers can be dilatory or opaque about sales/accounts. Negotiating timing of payment matters; small present sums can sometimes be extracted by bargaining on timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to newspapers are unpaid unless you bargain
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man who writes a single letter to a newspaper of course is not paid for it,--nor for any number of letters on some point personal to himself. I have since written sets of letters to newspapers, and have been paid for them; but then I have bargained for a price.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you expect payment for newspaper pieces, negotiate terms in advance rather than relying on implicit remuneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playwriting: must open dramatically and characters must win sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding criticism of his play: “I did not think it opened dramatically ... 'Margaret, my child, never play the jilt again; 'tis a most unbecoming character. Play it with what skill you will, it meets but little sympathy.' ... as a manager ... it is not a play I could have recommended for production.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play should have a strong dramatic opening and characters whose actions elicit audience sympathy; failing those, even well-crafted dialogue or scenes may not save a piece from rejection by managers or audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors guard publications; submissions must recommend themselves in style, matter, and length
rubrics_metrics.description: Meeting John Forster: submissions would be accepted “if the letters should recommend themselves by their style and matter, if they were not too long, and if ... this and if that, they should be favourably entertained.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When pitching to editors, ensure concise length, appropriate style and substantive matter; be prepared for editorial conditions and possible delays or non-response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise conscientiously (copy, re-copy, touch here and there)
rubrics_metrics.description: On his play: “I copied it, and re-copied it, touching it here and touching it there, and then sent it to my very old friend ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent revision and polishing are part of producing stronger work; multiple pass-throughs can improve dialogue and scenes even if larger structural issues remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance: continue producing work despite setbacks
rubrics_metrics.description: “But by continuing I could lose only pen and paper; and if the one chance in twenty did turn up in my favour, then how much might I win!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept early failures as part of a long-term career; continued effort can eventually yield success — the downside of persisting is relatively small compared to potential gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fieldwork and direct questioning for truthful reportage
rubrics_metrics.description: On investigating postal complaints: the practice was to send a servant to see complainant; Trollope describes startling people into revelations: “Unless I came down suddenly ... the very people who were robbed by our messengers would not confess the robbery ... It was necessary to startle them into the revelations which I required them to make ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For accurate reportage or portrait of life (useful to writers producing realistic material), direct observation and candid, sometimes abrupt, inquiry can be necessary to uncover truthful material.
